claim: Temporal binding has been understood as an illusion in timing judgment.
source: Temporal binding has been understood as an illusion in timing judgment.
evidence: This is a statement about how temporal binding has been conceptualized in the literature, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: When an action triggers an outcome after a brief delay, the action is reported to occur later than if the outcome does not occur.
source: When an action triggers an outcome (e.g. a sound) after a brief delay, the action is reported to occur later than if the outcome does not occur
evidence: This describes the action binding component of temporal binding, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The outcome is reported to occur earlier than a similar outcome not caused by an action.
source: the outcome is reported to occur earlier than a similar outcome not caused by an action
evidence: This describes the outcome binding component of temporal binding, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: An attention mechanism underlies the seeming illusion of timing judgment.
source: We show here that an attention mechanism underlies the seeming illusion of timing judgment.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by experimental data from four experiments.

claim: Visual spatial attention is critically involved in shaping event time reports made with the clock method.
source: We find that visual spatial attention is critically involved in shaping event time reports made in this way.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlations between attention measures and timing reports.

claim: Action and outcome events result in shifts of attention around the clock rim, thereby biasing the perceived location of the clock hand.
source: This occurs because action and outcome events result in shifts of attention around the clock rim, thereby biasing the perceived location of the clock hand.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data showing different attention distributions in different conditions.

claim: There is a difference in the distribution of visual spatial attention between a single-event condition and a two-event agency condition.
source: Using a probe detection task to measure attention, we show a difference in the distribution of visual spatial attention between a single-event condition (sound only or action only) and a two-event agency condition (action plus sound).
evidence: This is demonstrated through probe detection rate data in Experiments 1-4.

claim: Participants report the timing of the same event differently in single-event versus two-event conditions due to spatial attentional shifts.
source: Participants accordingly report the timing of the same event (the sound or the action) differently in the two conditions: spatial attentional shifts masquerading as temporal binding.
evidence: This is supported by timing report data showing differences between conditions that correlate with attention measures.

claim: Computational modeling based on the attention measure can reproduce the temporal binding effect.
source: Furthermore, computational modeling based on the attention measure can reproduce the temporal binding effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results showing significant correlations between modeled and actual binding effects.

claim: Outcome binding has a much bigger effect size than action binding.
source: Temporal binding is comprised of action binding (i.e. the action being reported as occurring later) and outcome binding (i.e. the sensory event being reported as occurring earlier), with outcome binding having a much bigger effect size (Haggard et al., 2002; Wolpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The temporal binding effect has attracted cross-disciplinary attention over the past two decades.
source: Over the two past decades, the temporal binding effect has attracted cross-disciplinary attention with regard to its cognitive/neural mechanisms and the potential applications especially with its widespread use as an implicit measure of sense of agency (Antusch et al., 2021; Buehner and Humphreys, 2009; Dogge et al., 2012; Haggard, 2017; Kirsch et al., 2019; Legaspi and Toyoizumi, 2019; Moore and Obhi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The impact of visuospatial attention has been heavily overlooked when considering the measurement of time judgment with the clock method.
source: However, the impact of visuospatial attention has been heavily overlooked when considering the measurement of time judgment with the widely used clock method (known as the Libet clock method; Libet et al., 1983; Wundt, 1874).
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review and the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: The clock method essentially transforms a timing task to a spatial localization task.
source: This essentially transforms a timing task to a spatial localization task.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the clock method based on how it requires participants to report spatial positions.

claim: Attention plays an important role in spatial localization.
source: It is well-known that attention plays an important role in spatial localization (Fortenbaugh and Robertson, 2011; Tse et al., 2011; Visser and Enns, 2001; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research.

claim: When the location of an object is ambiguous, participants tend to localize the object to the place where attention is directed.
source: When the location of an object is ambiguous, participants tend to localize the object to the place where attention is directed to Adam et al., 2008; Binda et al., 2009; Kirsch, 2015.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fast rotating clock hand makes the location report a challenging task.
source: This is particularly relevant to the temporal binding effect measured with the clock method, as the fast rotating clock hand makes the location report a challenging task (Haggard and Cole, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is also a logical inference about task difficulty.

claim: Action modulates the distribution of attention according to the action goal.
source: Previous research has provided ample evidence that action modulates the distribution of attention according to the action goal (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Rolfs et al., 2011; Humphreys et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When reaching towards a target, visual attention is drawn towards the target before the onset of the reaching action.
source: For example, when reaching towards a target, visual attention was shown to be drawn towards the target before the onset of the reaching action (Baldauf and Deubel, 2010; Deubel et al., 1998; Eimer et al., 2006; Rolfs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A clear outcome binding effect was confirmed in Experiment 1.
source: A clear outcome binding effect was confirmed in Experiment 1 (t(17) = 9.78, p<0.001, dz = 2.30, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 1.21e6; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The reported time was earlier when the sound was triggered by participants through a keypress than when the sound was controlled by the computer in Experiment 1.
source: The reported time was earlier when the sound was triggered by participants through a keypress (AS condition; M = –79.31 ms, 95% CI = [–102.93 –55.68] ms) than when the sound was controlled by the computer (SO condition; M = 34.17 ms, 95% CI = [12.73 55.60] ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The pattern of visuospatial attention distribution around the onset of the sound was drastically different between AS and SO conditions in Experiment 1.
source: Crucially, the pattern of visuospatial attention distribution around the onset of the sound (i.e. the event being judged), operationalized as the probe detection rate, was drastically different between the two conditions (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In the SO condition, the detection rate was low before the sound play but high after.
source: In the SO condition, the detection rate was low before the sound play (referring to both the clock hand locations and the time before the sound play), but high after.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data from Experiment 1.

claim: In the AS condition, the detection rate was high at the time of keypress, gradually increased, and peaked just before the sound play.
source: In the AS condition, the detection rate was high at the time of keypress, gradually increased, and peaked just before the sound play.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data from Experiment 1.

claim: After the sound play in the AS condition, the detection rate underwent a sharp decrease.
source: After the sound play, the detection rate underwent a sharp decrease.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data from Experiment 1.

claim: The attention distribution difference between AS and SO conditions was confirmed with a significant interaction effect in Experiment 1.
source: The attention distribution difference was confirmed with a significant interaction effect in a two-way (condition: AS vs. SO; probe location: –50°, –30°, –10°, 10°, 30°, and 50°) within-participants ANOVA comparing the detection rate (F(5,85) = 12.44, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.42, BFincl = 1.87e8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of probe detection data.

claim: A clear outcome binding effect was confirmed in Experiment 2.
source: Again, a clear outcome binding effect was confirmed (t(13) = 6.15, p<0.001, dz = 1.64, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 1.45e3; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The reported time was earlier in the AS condition than in the SO condition in Experiment 2.
source: The reported time was earlier in the AS condition (M = –46.61 ms, 95% CI = [–85.29 –7.93] ms) than in the SO condition (M = 47.86 ms, 95% CI = [22.15 73.57] ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The pattern of visual detection performance in Experiment 2 was almost identical to that found in Experiment 1.
source: The pattern of visual detection performance was almost identical to that found in Experiment 1 where there was no eye movement control.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of probe detection data between Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The two-way ANOVA in Experiment 2 confirmed a significant interaction effect between condition and probe location.
source: The two-way (condition: AS vs. SO; probe location: –50°, –30°, –10°, 10°, 30°, and 50°) within-participants ANOVA comparing the detection rate confirmed a significant interaction effect (F(5,65) = 4.18, p=0.013, ηp2 = 0.24, BFincl = 32.91).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of probe detection data from Experiment 2.

claim: No binding was found between VS and AS conditions in Experiment 3.
source: Indeed, no binding was found between VS and AS conditions (t(38) = 1.04, p=0.305, dz = 0.17, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 0.29; AS condition: M = –65.19 ms, 95% CI = [−87.80 –42.59] ms; VS condition: M = –40.96 ms, 95% CI = [–87.41 5.49] ms; Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The size of binding in Experiment 3 was smaller than in Experiments 1 & 2.
source: The size of binding in Experiment 3 (as calculated in Experiments 1 & 2) was smaller than in Experiments 1 & 2 (t(69) = –2.99, p=0.002, ds = –0.71, one-tailed unpaired t-test, BF-0 = 19.56).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of binding effects across experiments.

claim: The pattern of attention distribution appeared similar between VS and AS conditions in Experiment 3.
source: The pattern of attention distribution also appeared similar between VS and AS conditions. In both conditions, attention was high before the sound onset, but low after (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The action binding effect was confirmed in Experiment 4.
source: The action binding effect was confirmed (t(22) = 3.45, p=0.001, dz = 0.72, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 34.64; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The reported keypress time was later in the AS condition than in the AO condition in Experiment 4.
source: The reported keypress time was later in the AS condition (M = 102.28 ms, 95% CI = [86.06 118.50] ms) than in the SO condition (M = 78.37 ms, 95% CI = [58.91 97.83] ms).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: There was a significant difference in the attention distribution between AS and AO conditions in Experiment 4.
source: As predicted, there was a significant difference in the attention distribution between the two conditions, which was confirmed by a significant interaction effect in the two-way (condition: AS vs. AO; probe location: –50°, –40°, –30°, –20°, –10°, 0°, 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°, and 50°) within-participants ANOVA comparing the detection rate (F(10,220) = 2.93, p=0.026, ηp2 = 0.12, BFincl = 18.06).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of probe detection data from Experiment 4.

claim: After the sound onset in Experiment 4, the amount of attention resource was numerically higher in the AS condition than in the AO condition.
source: After the sound onset, the amount of attention resource was numerically higher in the AS condition than in the AO condition.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data from Experiment 4.

claim: The modeled timing report significantly correlated with the actual timing report in the AS condition of outcome binding.
source: In the AS condition of outcome binding (Experiments 1–3), a significant positive correlation was found between the modeled timing report of the sound and the actual timing report of the sound (r(65) = 0.55, p<0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, 4 outliers removed, BF+0 = 4.32e3, Figure 5b; without removing outliers: r(69) = 0.51, p<0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, BF+0 = 2.05e3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of modeling results and experimental data.

claim: A significant correlation was found between modeled and actual timing reports in the SO condition.
source: The same correlation was also found in the SO condition (here the SO condition from Experiments 1 & 2 and the VS condition from Experiment 3 were combined) (r(65) = 0.36, p=0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, four outliers removed, BF+0 = 19.16, Figure 5c; without removing outliers: r(69) = 0.26, p=0.014, one-tailed Spearman correlation, BF+0 = 2.83).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of modeling results and experimental data.

claim: For action binding, a significant correlation was found between the modeled timing report and the actual timing report in both AS and AO conditions.
source: For the timing report of the keypress (Experiment 4), a significant correlation was found between the modeled timing report and the actual timing report in both AS condition (r(21) = 0.43, p=0.021, one-tailed Spearman correlation, BF+0 = 4.78, Figure 5e; no outlier detected) and AO condition (r(20) = 0.72, p<0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, one outlier removed, BF+0 = 240.40, Figure 5f; without removing outliers: r(21) = 0.74, p<0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, BF+0 = 391.20).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of modeling results and experimental data.

claim: A significant correlation was found between the modeled outcome binding effect and the actual outcome binding effect.
source: For outcome binding (Experiments 1–3), a significant correlation was found between the modeled effect and the actual effect (r(69) = 0.43, p<0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, no outliers found, BF+0 = 199.22, Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of modeling results and experimental data.

claim: A significant correlation was found between the modeled action binding effect and the actual action binding effect.
source: For action binding (Experiment 4), a similar correlation was found (r(20) = 0.60, p=0.002, one-tailed Spearman correlation, one outlier removed, BF+0 = 16.28, Figure 5g; without removing outliers: r(21) = 0.60, p=0.001, one-tailed Spearman correlation, BF+0 = 17.87).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of modeling results and experimental data.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 1 was statistically significant.
source: In Experiment 1, the modeled outcome binding effect (M = 75.97 ms) was statistically significant (t(17) = 3.98, p<0.001, dz = 0.94, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 77.53; Figure 5h)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of modeling results.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 1 showed a marginally significant reduction compared to the actual outcome binding effect.
source: but showed a marginally significant reduction compared to the actual outcome binding effect (M = 113.47 ms; t(17) = –2.01, p=0.061, dz = 0.47, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 1.24).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modeled and actual effects.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 2 was statistically significant.
source: In Experiment 2, the modeled outcome binding effect (M = 41.23 ms) was statistically significant (t(13) = 3.22, p=0.003, dz = 0.86, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 15.74; Figure 5i)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of modeling results.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 2 was significantly smaller than the actual outcome binding effect.
source: but significantly smaller than the actual outcome binding effect (M = 94.46 ms; t(13) = –3.61, p=0.003, dz = –0.96, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 14.61).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modeled and actual effects.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 3 was not statistically significant.
source: The modeled outcome binding effect was also not significant (M = –14.94 ms, t(38) = 1.61, p=0.116, dz = 0.26, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 0.56; Figure 5j).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of modeling results.

claim: There was no significant difference between the modeled and actual outcome binding effects in Experiment 3.
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the modeled and actual effects (t(38) = –1.72, p=0.093, dz = –0.28, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 0.66).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modeled and actual effects.

claim: The modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 3 was significantly smaller than the modeled outcome binding in Experiments 1 & 2.
source: Importantly, like the actual outcome binding effect showed earlier, the modeled outcome binding effect in Experiment 3 was significantly smaller than the modeled outcome binding in Experiments 1 & 2 (t(69) = –5.00, p<0.001, ds = –1.19, one-tailed unpaired t-test, BF-0 = 7.44e3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modeling results across experiments.

claim: The modeled action binding effect in Experiment 4 was statistically significant.
source: In Experiment 4, the modeled action binding effect (M = 10.83 ms) was statistically significant (t(22) = 2.16, p=0.021, dz = 0.45, one-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF+0 = 2.97; Figure 5k)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of modeling results.

claim: The modeled action binding effect in Experiment 4 was significantly smaller than the actual action binding effect.
source: and significantly smaller than the actual action binding effect (M = 23.91 ms; t(22) = –2.17, p=0.041, dz = –0.45, two-tailed paired-samples t-test, BF10 = 1.53).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modeled and actual effects.

claim: Visuospatial attention has a direct link to the event timing report, with the reported time corresponding to the location on the clock where attention was paid to.
source: In four complementary experiments, it was demonstrated that visuospatial attention had a direct link to the event timing report, with the reported time corresponding to the location on the clock where attention was paid to.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between attention measures and timing reports across all experiments.

claim: Action and sensory input both can activate the concentration of attention to the clock.
source: Action and sensory input both can activate the concentration of attention to the clock, resulting in a dynamic attention distribution pattern around the event which requires a timing report.
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data showing attention changes following actions and sensory events.

claim: The difference in the attention distribution pattern activated by action and sensory input contributes massively to the temporal binding effect.
source: Critically, the difference in the attention distribution pattern activated by action and sensory input contributes massively to the temporal binding effect.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between attention differences and binding effects, and by the modeling results.

claim: The attention account provides at least a partial explanation for both outcome binding and action binding in terms of a bias in the distribution of visuospatial attention.
source: The attention account provides at least a partial explanation for both outcome binding and action binding in terms of a bias in the distribution of visuospatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing attention's role in both types of binding.

claim: The role of attention in the event timing measure with the clock method has long been speculated.
source: It should be noted that the role of attention in the event timing measure with the clock method has long been speculated (Haggard and Cole, 2007; Libet, 1985; Libet et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When the event that required a timing judgment was held in attention, the timing report was more accurate than when the event was not held in attention.
source: For example, Haggard and Cole, 2007 showed that when the event that required a timing judgment at the end of a trial was held in attention (participants knew which event to be judged before the event actually occurred), the timing report was more accurate than when the event was not held in attention (participants did not know which event to be judged until the event occurred).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haggard and Cole, 2007.

claim: Hon (2023) proposed that the attentional resources required to predict action outcomes might be the cause of action binding.
source: Hon, 2023 recently proposed the idea that the attentional resources required to predict action outcomes might be the cause of action binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hon, 2023.

claim: Schwarz and Weller (2023) discussed the possibility that the sharing of attentional resources between two events resulted in less attention being paid to the event that required timing judgment, thereby leading to temporal binding.
source: In a similar vein, Schwarz and Weller, 2023 discussed the possibility that the sharing of attentional resources between two events (action and sound) in the instrumental condition resulted in less attention being paid to the event that required timing judgment as compared to the one event baseline condition, thereby leading to temporal binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz and Weller, 2023.

claim: A color change of the clock hand, which was supposed to consume attentional resources, could also lead to the pattern of temporal binding.
source: Experimental evidence was provided showing that a color change of the clock hand, which was supposed to consume attentional resources, could also lead to the pattern of temporal binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research (implied from context).

claim: The visuospatial attention to the clock face has a direct influence on the localization of the clock hand.
source: The present study explicitly pointed out that the visuospatial attention to the clock face had a direct influence on the localization of the clock hand (i.e. the reported event timing).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing correlations between attention and timing reports.

claim: It is unlikely that a changed timing judgment leads to a changed attention distribution, at least in outcome binding.
source: It is unlikely that a changed timing judgment leads to a changed attention distribution, at least in outcome binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of events in the experiments.

claim: In the outcome binding test, the attention activation following the keypress in the AS condition was before the sound onset.
source: In the outcome binding test, the attention activation following the keypress in the AS condition was before the sound onset, i.e., before the event that requires timing judgment (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: This is supported by probe detection data shown in Figures 3b and 3d.

claim: Timing judgment is a constructive process which integrates available information from both before and after the event of interest.
source: Since timing judgment is a constructive process which integrates available information from both before and after the event of interest (Cao et al., 2020; Haggard et al., 2002; Klaffehn et al., 2021; Moore and Haggard, 2008; Takahata et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The modeled temporal binding effect is smaller than the measured effect.
source: However, the modeled temporal binding effect is smaller than the measured effect (Figure 5i and k).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Figures 5i and 5k.

claim: The impact of attention may not have been fully captured in the current study.
source: However, the impact of attention may not have been fully captured in the current study.
evidence: This is speculation based on the limitations of the experimental design.

claim: Attention was only measured in a limited spatial area (100° starting with the clock hand position at the keypress time).
source: First, attention was only measured in a limited spatial area (100° starting with the clock hand position at the keypress time).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Attention outside the measured area may also contribute to the timing report.
source: In fact, attention outside this area may also contribute to the timing report.
evidence: This is speculation about potential unmeasured factors.

claim: The spatial attention to the locations where the clock hand pointed to at the action preparation stage may have a strong influence on the timing report.
source: The spatial attention to the locations where the clock hand pointed to at the action preparation stage especially may have a strong influence on the timing report.
evidence: This is speculation about potential unmeasured factors.

claim: Experiment 3 provided causal evidence that attention drives the outcome binding effect.
source: Experiment 3 provided causal evidence that attention drives the outcome binding effect, as outcome binding was not statistically significant when the attention difference was experimentally controlled for between contrasting conditions (with a doubled sample size).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental manipulation and results of Experiment 3.

claim: Temporal binding declined when the temporal predictability of action and effect was controlled for.
source: Previous research also showed that temporal binding declined when the temporal predictability of action and effect was controlled for (Kirsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 2019.

claim: The cognitive underpinnings of temporal binding is currently still an open question.
source: Therefore, the cognitive underpinnings of temporal binding is currently still an open question.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of the study's findings and limitations.

claim: Wundt was probably the first to use the clock with a fast rotating hand for the scientific study of mental chronometry.
source: Wundt was probably the first to use the clock with a fast rotating hand for the scientific study of mental chronometry (Wundt, 1874).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wundt, 1874, and represents historical knowledge.

claim: The method is now also known as the Libet clock method, as Libet popularised this method in his famous study on free will.
source: The method is now also known as the Libet clock method, as Libet popularised this method in his famous study on free will (Libet et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Libet et al., 1983, and represents historical knowledge.

claim: The timing report results from the clock method are quite variable among individuals.
source: It is known that the timing report results from this method are quite variable among individuals and strongly depend on the method details such as the speed of the clock hand (Ivanof et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2010; Pockett and Miller, 2007; Sanford, 1974; Seifried et al., 2010; Wundt, 1874; Yabe and Goodale, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Any difference between conditions in the timing report from the clock method may be due to (or at least confounded by) differences in spatial attention.
source: The current study suggests that any difference between conditions in the timing report from this method may be in fact due to (or at least confounded by) differences in spatial attention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings about attention's role in timing reports.

claim: A full picture of the spatiotemporal visual attention distribution is still waiting to be revealed in the timing report task with the clock method.
source: First, as mentioned before, a full picture of the spatiotemporal visual attention distribution is still waiting to be revealed in the timing report task with the clock method.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future research needs.

claim: The clock method may not be an optimal tool for resolving the issue of a timing judgment component in temporal binding.
source: Second, the clock method may not be an optimal tool for resolving the issue of a timing judgment component in temporal binding.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the clock method.

claim: Even if attention could fully account for the temporal binding effect measured with the clock, it could also mean that the timing judgment component could not be easily measured in this way.
source: Even if attention could fully account for the temporal binding effect measured with the clock, it could also mean that the timing judgment component could not be easily measured in this way (Stetson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative interpretations of the findings.

claim: Temporal binding has been demonstrated using paradigms in which visual attention does not seem to be critically involved.
source: Indeed, temporal binding has also been demonstrated using paradigms in which visual attention does not seem to be critically involved, including but not limited to the interval estimation paradigm (Engbert et al., 2007; Humphreys and Buehner, 2009) and the auditory timer paradigm (Martinez et al., 2018; Muth et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research using different paradigms.

claim: Attention is critically involved in temporal binding, at least when the measurement process involves attention.
source: Attention is critically involved in temporal binding, at least when the measurement process involves attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: It is important to discount the contribution of attention in a clock-like method study before drawing conclusions about the temporal properties in cognition.
source: It is important to discount the contribution of attention in a clock-like method study before drawing conclusions about the temporal properties in cognition.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings about attention's confounding role.

claim: 20 participants were recruited for Experiment 1.
source: 20 participants (11 females; mean age = 21.2, SD = 1.8) were recruited from a local participant pool.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: 18 participants should lead to a statistical power of 0.98 for detecting outcome binding.
source: Assuming an effect size of 0.89 (note that this is the effect size of outcome binding and action binding combined as reported in a meta-analysis, see Tanaka et al., 2019. Since outcome binding has a larger effect size than action binding, the real effect size of outcome binding should be larger than this), 18 participants (two excluded in the formal data analysis, see below) should lead to a statistical power of 0.98 (alpha = 0.05; one-tailed) (Faul et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a power analysis calculation based on previous literature.

claim: The experiment was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013).
source: The experiment was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013) and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology and Behavioural Sciences, Zhejiang University (ethics application number: [2022]003).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: The clock hand rotated at 1800 ms per revolution.
source: In each trial, participants watched a clock face (diameter: 2.7° of visual angle, dva) with a clock hand rapidly rotating clockwise (1800 ms per revolution).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus.

claim: A sound was presented with a delay of 250 ms after the keypress.
source: After the keypress, a visual probe (a disk with a diameter of 0.1 dva) and a sound (1000 Hz tone, 50 ms long, 5 ms rise/fall envelop, comfortable volume level) were both presented with a delay of 250 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Visual probes were presented at six possible locations in the outcome binding experiments.
source: Visual probes were presented at six possible locations (corresponding to sic time points): –50° (–250 ms; this is when the keypress was made in the AS condition), –30° (–150 ms), –10° (–50 ms), 10° (50 ms), 30° (150 ms), and 50° (250 ms) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There were 50 catch trials, 50 timing report trials, and 180 visual probe trials in each condition of Experiments 1 and 2.
source: There were 50 catch trials, 50 timing report trials, and 180 visual probe trials (30 trials for each visual probe location/timing).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A new group of 20 participants were recruited for Experiment 2.
